questions.q: Why is the RGB light system called additive?
options: Because colours are added in layers of ink
Because the three primaries together create all the hues in the spectrum
Because it adds black to every colour
Because it is used only for printing
questions.explain: CMYK printing works the opposite way — inks subtract light.
questions.evidence: This light system is called additive because the three primaries together create all the hues in the spectrum.

questions.q: How many colour systems must designers be aware of, often in the same project?
questions.explain: Screens use RGB light; print uses CMYK inks.
questions.evidence: it is important to realize that there are two colour systems, and often a project needs to work in both.

questions.q: What is emphasis in composition?
options: Making a specific element gain the attention of the eye
questions.explain: Contrast in size, colour or position creates emphasis.
questions.evidence: This is called emphasis and is achieved by making a specific element gain the attention of the eye.

questions.q: When is a single-column grid an excellent approach?
options: When the content is formatted in a simple manner
Never — grids should always have several columns
questions.explain: Choose the grid to suit the structure of the content.
questions.evidence: A single-column grid is an excellent approach if the content a designer is working with is formatted in a simple manner

questions.q: In communication design, how does what you say relate to how you say it?
options: What you are saying determines how you say it and how it is delivered
questions.explain: Message first, then form and delivery.
questions.evidence: what you are saying determines how you say it and in turn how it is delivered to your audience.

questions.q: How should colour be thought of in graphic reproduction?
options: As a fixed property of ink
As a number in a file
As an event rather than an attribute of an object
questions.explain: A light source, an object and an observer must all take part.
questions.evidence: learn to think of colour as an event rather than as an attribute or characteristic of a particular object.

questions.q: Why is colour described as an event?
options: It requires three components to take part at a particular point in time
It depends on the price of ink
questions.explain: Change the light, the surface or the viewer and the colour changes.
questions.evidence: Colour is an event because it requires the participation of three components at a particular point in time to take place.

questions.q: What is the perceptual rendering intent mainly used for?
options: RGB to CMYK transformations, typically image conversions
questions.explain: Colorimetric intents clip out-of-gamut colours instead.
questions.evidence: The perceptual intent is used mainly for RGB to CMYK transformations, which are typically image conversions.

questions.q: What is trapping in prepress?
options: Locking a file so it can't be edited
An electronic file treatment that helps solve registration issues on certain press technologies
Converting images to black and white
questions.explain: Slight overlaps between abutting colours hide small misregistration on press.
questions.evidence: It is an electronic file treatment that must be performed to help solve registration issues on certain kinds of press technologies.

questions.q: What is paper opacity?
options: The degree to which light is prevented from travelling through the paper
questions.explain: Opacity matters most for thin stocks printed on both sides.
questions.evidence: opacity is the degree to which light is prevented from travelling through a paper.

questions.q: What was blackletter?
options: The medieval model for the first movable types
A modern sans-serif made for screens
A typeface designed for road signs
questions.explain: Its condensed letterforms give a very dark page tone.
questions.evidence: Blackletter was the medieval model for the first movable types

questions.q: Why is a page set in blackletter hard to read?
options: Legibility was not its first function — books were objects of wealth and beauty
questions.explain: Today legibility comes first.
questions.evidence: The look of the letterforms makes it hard to read the page, because legibility was not their first function as it is today.

questions.q: What are the four kinds of horizontal text alignment?
options: Flush left, flush right, centred and fully justified
questions.explain: Flush left is also called ragged right.
questions.evidence: Typographically, horizontal alignment includes flush left

questions.q: What is the baseline grid in layout software?
options: The invisible line on which font characters sit
questions.explain: Aligning text to it keeps lines consistent across columns.
questions.evidence: A baseline grid exists in digital software that is meant for layout of type and is the invisible line where font characters sit.

questions.q: Which colours are warm colours?
questions.explain: Cool colours are blue, green and purple.
questions.evidence: Warm colours are the red, orange, and yellow colours of the colour wheel, while cool colours are blue, green, and purple.

questions.q: Why are grids often used in publication and web design?
options: They bring consistency and guide hierarchy
questions.explain: A complex grid can still leave room for new elements.
questions.evidence: Grids are often used in publication and web design because they introduce consistency and guide hierarchy.

questions.q: What should the grid for a book of poetry provide?
options: Generous negative space and generous leading
questions.explain: The grid should suit the content it carries.
questions.evidence: if your publication is a book of poetry, the grid must have generous amounts of negative space and generous leading

questions.q: What is the information gathered in the first stage of the design process?
options: The final brief that can't change
Just a starting point — more research fine-tunes the goals
questions.explain: Research continues as the problem becomes clearer.
questions.evidence: The information you collected in the first stage is just a starting point

questions.q: Why is research before concept development so important?
options: It helps craft a message that gets the response the client needs
It replaces the need for concepts
It lets you skip the client
questions.explain: Knowing the audience shapes the message.
questions.evidence: Knowing this information before the concept development begins is vital to crafting a message that will generate the response your client needs.

questions.q: What do critiquing and analysis let a designer evaluate?
options: How much the client will pay
How effective the whole design is for the concept and problem
questions.explain: Critique is built into the iterative design process.
questions.evidence: Critiquing and analysis allow you to evaluate the effectiveness of the whole design in relation to the concept and problem.

questions.q: What does a strong concept help communicate?
options: The benefits of the offer and how it differs from the competition
questions.explain: A concept carries the message, not just the decoration.
questions.evidence: It helps to communicate the benefits of the offer and helps with differentiation from the competition.

questions.q: When using hyperbole in visual communication, what must you ensure?
options: That it is a clear exaggeration
questions.explain: Otherwise viewers may take it literally.
questions.evidence: When used for visual communication, one must be careful to ensure that hyperbole is a clear exaggeration.

questions.q: After attracting attention, what must a design do next?
options: Hold the audience's interest long enough to absorb the whole message
questions.explain: It then needs to create desire and prompt action.
questions.evidence: Your design must hold the audience’s interest long enough so they can completely absorb the whole communication.

questions.q: Which three components must take part for colour to happen?
options: A screen, a cable and a computer
An object, light and an observer
questions.explain: That's why colour is described as an event.
questions.evidence: how the object, light, and observer contribute to the colour event

questions.q: Most objects are opaque. What does that mean for how we see their colour?
options: We see light passing through them
We mostly see light reflected from their surface
questions.explain: Transparent objects transmit light instead.
questions.evidence: The majority of objects are opaque, so most of the time we are dealing with the reflection of light.

questions.q: What are the CIE's three core definitions for colour?
options: The standard observer, the Lab colour space and Delta E
questions.explain: Lab and Delta E are especially important for colour management.
questions.evidence: Three core definitions provided by the CIE are the standard observer, the Lab colour space, and Delta E measurements.

questions.q: Why are there no negative values on the L axis of Lab colour space?
options: You can't have less than zero light, which is absolute darkness
Negative numbers are banned in colour science
questions.explain: L describes the amount of light; a and b describe its colour.
questions.evidence: there are no negative values on the L axis as we can’t have less than zero light, which describes absolute darkness

questions.q: What do the a and b axes describe in Lab colour space?
options: The colour character — the type of light
questions.explain: They are the chromatic axes.
questions.evidence: describing the colour character and the type of light

questions.q: How are the spots on a raster grid encoded?
options: Each is either on or off — binary 0 or 1
questions.explain: Raster image processing turns pages into these grids.
questions.evidence: The spots on the grid can only be turned on or off

questions.q: In computer-to-plate technology, what exposes the printing plate?
questions.explain: The laser exposes an emulsion on the plate.
questions.evidence: a laser is used to expose an emulsion on a printing plate

questions.q: Who pioneered the first device-independent font files with PostScript?
questions.explain: Microsoft later developed TrueType to compete.
questions.evidence: The development of the PostScript computer language was pioneered by Adobe in creating the first device independent font files.

questions.q: What does it usually mean if a font file has no kerning values?
options: It is a monospaced font only
It is a poor font that will cause spacing problems
questions.explain: Kerning adjusts space between specific letter pairs.
questions.evidence: If no kerning value appears, the font is usually a poor one and will cause spacing problems in the document it is used in.

questions.q: When must you pay close attention to reproducing an exact hue from device to device?
options: Only when viewing on one screen
When printing graphics onto a substrate
questions.explain: Designers must use colour models proven to give the same results on different devices.
questions.evidence: It is only when we image a computer graphic on a substrate that we must pay attention to rendering the exact hue of red from one device to another.

questions.q: Why is a swatch book only an approximate guide to final colour?
options: It fades over time and its paper doesn't match every substrate
questions.explain: Colour depends on the substrate as well as the ink.
questions.evidence: the swatch books fade over time

questions.q: Where do most registration errors happen on a printing press?
options: As the substrate travels from one printing unit to the next
questions.explain: Trapping compensates for these tiny misalignments.
questions.evidence: The substrate must travel from one printing unit to the next, and it is here that most registration errors occur.

questions.q: What is the extra element created by trapping called?
questions.explain: It overlaps adjoining colours slightly to hide gaps.
questions.evidence: That third element is called a trap line

questions.q: What is the main concern when transparent elements are rasterised in a PDF?
options: They print in black and white
They can no longer be edited
questions.explain: So transparency levels must be right before rasterising.
questions.evidence: The primary concern is that the elements rasterized in the PDF are no longer editable

questions.q: Is what you see on screen a reliable guide to transparency in the final output?
questions.explain: Operators need to know when WYSIWYG isn't adequate.
questions.evidence: what we are viewing on a computer screen is not necessarily a good representation of the final output

questions.q: What is preflight?
options: Checking a graphic document before it goes to manufacturing
questions.explain: Preflight catches problems before they become expensive.
questions.evidence: The task of checking a computer graphic document in preparation for the manufacturing process is called preflight.

questions.q: What does 'creep' do in imposition?
options: Moves page images closer to the spine to allow for the publication's thickness
questions.explain: Inner pages of a saddle-stitched booklet stick out further when folded.
questions.evidence: Creep pushes the image on a page closer in to the spine the further the page is toward the spine

questions.q: What is a paper's basis weight?
options: The weight of 500 sheets at its parent sheet size
questions.explain: 80# cover means 500 parent-size sheets weigh 80 pounds.
questions.evidence: Basis weight is the weight of 500 sheets of paper at a specific size

questions.q: Why are colour prints usually done on 24# or 28# bond instead of 20#?
questions.explain: Heavier stock stops colour showing through to the other side.
questions.evidence: colour prints are more commonly done on 24# or 28# bond due to the need for higher opacity
